text: A reminder, in plain text, of what I think humans actually bring to the table now that the machines are very good and getting better every day. I keep coming back to the word "taste" and I keep finding it too small. Taste is the surface. There is a whole engine underneath it, and that engine is the part the model can't have. Yet. Maybe ever. I don't know. I'm not in that argument. I'm in this one: Models are trained on the average. The average is the floor, not the ceiling. Our job is not to conform a little better than the last person who conformed. Our job is to know the rule cold, and then break it on purpose, in public, with a reason. Symmetry is a rule. Break it. Three-act structure is a rule. Break it. "Don't shoot into the sun" is a rule. Break it. If you can't say why you broke it, you didn't break it, you just missed. Inspiration does not live in the first ten image-search results. It lives in: A model averages the internet. A human walks somewhere strange and brings back something unexpected. Every brief now has an invisible third party at the table. Someone has to keep saying "and what does this feel like for the person on the other end of it." Someone has to keep saying "how is humanity better through the birthing of this idea?" That's the job. Not "is it on-brand." Not "does it convert." What does it feel like? what good does it do? If you aren't there saying it, no one will. The model certainly won't. Tension. Surprise. Restraint. The pause before the punchline. The photograph that's almost in focus. The sentence that ends one beat earlier than you expected. These are not bugs. These are the entire reason anyone remembers anything. "Correct" is the lowest bar in the building. Step over it and keep walking. I would rather make one thing that makes someone laugh out loud on a train than ten things that "meet the brief." At the very least, it needs to make ME laugh. This is a personal bias. If it's not at least a little bit fun, why are we here? A working sketch beats a confident take. Every time. A bad first draft beats a brilliant unwritten one. Every time. A weird little prototype beats a slide deck about prototyping. Every. Time. Make 50 things. Throw away 47. Talk about the 3. Do not, under any circumstances, become a person who mostly posts opinions about other people's work. If the AI output is bad, the AI did not fail you. You failed it. You picked the tool. You wrote the prompt. You accepted the result. You shipped it. The fix is not a better model, or a return to tools of the past. The fix is a sharper you. Sharpen yourself. Sharpen your ideas. Sharpen the way you say what you mean, because the gap between what you wanted and what came back is almost always a gap in you , not in the tool. Powerful tools reward the people who showed up sharp, iterate, spend extra time on the vision. They expose the people who didn't. AI is not the great equalizer, it is the great amplifier. Watching the generation happen is not the work. Prompting once and accepting the result is not the work. The work is the back-and-forth. The push. The loop. The "again, but tweak is this way..." The hundredth iteration where the thing finally clicks. If you're a spectator to your own output, you are not the author of your own output. Get your hands in. Both. At the same time. Some days the play is in service of a thing. Some days the play is the thing. A practice that only ever has goals is a job. A practice that never has goals is a hobby. The good work lives in between. Play doesn't result in burnout. It results in excitement, happiness, experiment, the unexpected, and an urge to play more. The split is fake. It was always fake. It's especially fake now. The people who can think of the thing and make the thing are going to eat. The people who can only do one half are going to be very busy explaining why the other half is hard, or blame the processes or tools. Don't be that person. Learn the other half. It's never been cheaper to learn it. This file will be wrong in six months. That is fine. I'd rather be specifically wrong than vaguely correct. — b. last touched, kitchen table, late.
